papers.title_in_file: Graph Neural Networks on Quantum Computers
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proposes quantum circuit constructions for graph convolutional, graph attention and message-passing GNNs and analyses the time and space complexity of quantum SGC and LGC against classical ones, with no experiments.

existing.note: The stored value drops the end of the sentence: the paper places the empirical evaluations 'in more general settings and real-world applications'. The paper also says outright that it does no benchmark evaluation (Appendix E, p.47), which the stored id implies but the value does not say.
existing.value: The authors list further analysis and empirical evaluations to assess the performance and scalability of their Quantum GNN architectures in more general settings and real-world applications as future research directions, and state that, unlike Chen et al., who evaluate their QGCN on a benchmarking dataset, their own work focuses on the theoretical aspects and complexity analysis.
quotes: Future research directions include further analysis and empirical evaluations to assess the performance and scalability of our Quantum GNN architectures in more general settings and real-world applications.
While Chen et al. evaluate their QGCN on certain benchmarking dataset, our work focuses on the theoretical aspects and performed rigorous complexity analysis

assertions.value: The authors propose quantum algorithms corresponding to the three fundamental types of classical GNNs: Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Attention Networks and Message-Passing GNNs.
quotes: We devise quantum algorithms corresponding to the three fundamental types of classical GNNs: Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Attention Networks, and MessagePassing GNNs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of what it does, Abstract p.1.

assertions.value: The paper derives that the quantum SGC with minimum circuit depth has time complexity logarithmic in the input sizes, assuming fixed success probability, against the classical SGC's time complexity of order N d C plus N C squared; the space complexity of the quantum SGC in this case is comparable to the classical SGC's.
quotes: The time complexity of the quantum SGC in the case is logarithmic in the input sizes
(assuming fixed success probability), this represents a significant improvement over the classical SGC's time complexity of O(N dC + N C2)
However, the space complexity of quantum SGC in this case is comparable to that of the classical SGC.
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation, not a theorem; it rests on cited state-preparation and block-encoding costs.

assertions.value: The paper derives that the quantum SGC with minimum qubits has space complexity of order log(NC), an exponential reduction compared to the classical SGC's space complexity, and that its time complexity in this case still offers a computational advantage over the classical SGC, though less pronounced than in the minimum depth case.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.2, Case 2, p.13; Eq. (65) and (67), p.32
quotes: The space complexity of the quantum SGC in the minimum qubits case is O(log(N C)), which represents an exponential reduction compared to the classical SGC's space complexity
Furthermore, the time complexity of the quantum SGC, in this case, still offers a computational advantage over the classical SGC.
Although the speedup is less pronounced compared to the minimum depth case
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation, not a theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The minimum-qubit time bound in Eq. (65) still grows with NC divided by log(NC), so it is not logarithmic.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum SGC provides a probabilistic result with a success probability of 1 − δ, and that the complexity tables give quantum space as the number of qubits including ancilla qubits.
quotes: The quantum SGC provides a probabilistic result with a success probability of 1 − δ.
space complexity in the quantum case refers to the number of qubits, including the ancilla qubits used by the circuit
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the terms of its own comparison in Table 1's caption and note, p.13.

assertions.value: The authors state that intermediate choices of ancillary qubits could potentially lead to moderate improvements in both time and space complexity, and that this moderate case could be advantageous for hardware or problem instances where neither circuit depth nor qubit number is the sole limiting factor.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.2, p.13 (the formulas for the moderate case are scrambled in the text layer and were read from the page image); Eq. (62), p.31
quotes: which could potentially lead to m√oderate improve- me√nts
This moderate case could be advantageous for certain quantum hardware architectures or problem instances where neither the circuit depth nor the number of qubits is the sole limiting factor.

assertions.reader_inference: The page image shows square-root scaling in NC for both time and qubits in this case.

assertions.value: The authors assume that the depth of the PQC implementing the SGC weight matrix is less than the depth of the circuit for S to the K, prioritizing efficiency while potentially sacrificing some expressiveness in the weight matrix.
quotes: We assume that the depth of this PQC is less than the depth of the circuit for SK.
we prioritize the efficiency of the overall quantum SGC implementation while potentially sacrificing some expressiveness in the weight matrix
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated assumption, Section 3.2 p.12.

assertions.value: The authors encode node features by amplitude encoding with the state preparation method of reference [48], whose Theorem 3 gives a tunable trade-off between the number of ancillary qubits and the circuit depth.
quotes: We select the approach from Ref. [48] for our data encoding, as their work provides a tunable trade-off between the number of ancillary qubits and the circuit depth for the state preparation.
According to Theorem 3 in [48]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to reference 48.

assertions.value: The authors implement S squared for K = 2 as the product of block-encoded matrices, citing Lemma 53 of reference [62].
quotes: In the quantum SGC, for K = 2,10 we can efficiently implement SK by leveraging the product of block-encoded matrices as stated in Lemma 53 of Ref.[62]
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited lemma.

assertions.value: The authors cite the SGC work [55] for the claims that SGC removes nonlinearities while performing comparably to vanilla GCN, that the simplifications do not affect accuracy across various applications, and that SGC with K = 2 often matches or beats K > 2.
quotes: the experimental results demonstrated that the simplifications do not affect the accuracy across various applications [55]
SGC with K = 2 often achieves similar/better performance than that of K > 2 in many downstream applications.[55]
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited classical result.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [64], that although the N C squared term appears to dominate classical SGC time, node-wise feature transformation runs at reduced cost through parallel dense matrix multiplication, so the N d C term is the dominant term and the primary obstacle to scalability.
assertions.anchor: Table 1 caption, p.13; Table 4 caption, p.32
quotes: However, in practice, node-wise feature transformation can be executed at a reduced cost due to the parallelism in dense-dense matrix multiplications.
Consequently, O(N dC) is the dominant complexity term in the time complexity of classical SGC and the primary obstacle to achieving scalability [64].
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited claim about classical practice.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [77], that a K-layer classical GCN has time complexity of order K N C squared plus K |E| C and space complexity of order |E| plus K C squared plus K N C.
quotes: For K layers, the overall time complexity is O(KN C2 + K|E|C + KN ) = O(KN C2 + K|E|C). The space complexity is O(|E| + KC2 + KN C). [77]
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited complexity count.

assertions.value: The paper derives that the quantum LGC with minimum qubits has space complexity of order log(NC), significantly lower than classical LGC, and a time complexity that provides a potential advantage over classical LGC for certain problem instances.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.3, p.15; Table 2, p.15; Table 5, p.33
quotes: The space complexity of this case is O(log(N C)), which is significantly lower than the space complexity of classical LGC.
which also provides a potential advantage over classical LGC's O(KN dC + KN C2) for certain problem instances
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation, not a theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical LGC time is written with a K N C squared term in the text on p.15 but with N C squared in Table 2 (p.15), Eq. (70) and Table 5 (p.33).

assertions.value: The authors implement the LGC polynomial of the Laplacian with the polynomial eigenvalue transformation, a special instance of QSVT, so that the QSVT phases are the tunable weights to be trained; the depth for the block encoding of P(L) is K times the depth of the block-encoding of L plus the additional one- and two-qubit gates.
quotes: The parametrization of the polynomial is equivalent to parametrization of the Pauli angles(phases) in the QSVT circuit, that is, the phases are the tunable weights to be trained.
The depth of the circuit for the block encoding of P (L) is K times the depth of the block-encoding UL plus O((n′anc + 1)K) for the additional one- and two-qubit gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction and its depth count; the QSVT result is cited (Theorem 56 of ref. 66).

assertions.value: The authors state that their graph attention construction does not strictly achieve a block-encoding of the weighted adjacency matrix, but generates a quantum state that resembles the graph attention operation.
quotes: are not strictly constructing Oldiagonal here and the following operations do not strictly achieve a blockencoding of the weighted adjacency matrix
however the alternative versions do generate a quantum state that resembles the Graph attention operation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit, footnote 13 p.18.

assertions.value: The authors restrict the attention and message-passing constructions to graphs whose (weighted) adjacency matrices can be decomposed as the summation of 1-sparse matrices, with the sum over them carried out by LCU.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1, p.16; Section 4.2, p.17; Section 5, p.25
quotes: in this paper we investigate certain sparse matrices (here, the weighted adjacency matrices) that can be decomposed as the summation of 1-sparse matrices
we investigate the graphs with certain adjacency matrices that can be decomposed as the summation of 1-sparse matrices
The summation over l can be carried out by Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the class of graphs it treats, Sections 4.2 and 5.

assertions.value: The authors' quantum message-passing GNN relies on the update function being linear in its arguments, so that aggregation over neighbours is achieved by an overall LCU module.
quotes: Since φ is linear in its arguments, we have
This allows us to achieve the aggregation over different neighbours by the overall LCU module
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own construction assumption, Section 5 p.26.
assertions.reader_inference: The activation function is omitted from the update function here (footnote 15, p.24), which is what makes it linear.

assertions.value: The authors build a quantum attention oracle in which the attention score is the inner product of linearly transformed node features, evaluated in superposition by a parallel swap test and stored in a register by amplitude estimation.
quotes: this attention score can be evaluated on quantum circuit by parallel Swap Test
The second step is to use amplitude estimation [81] to extract and store the attention scores into an additional register
assertions.certainty_reason: A circuit construction without a cost analysis.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no complexity count for the attention or message-passing constructions; only SGC and LGC are analysed.

assertions.value: The authors show, by circuit identities in figures, that the selective copying operation can be implemented by a circuit with constant depth, as a comparing unitary followed by a controlled copy.
assertions.anchor: Appendix A, Figs. 13 to 17, p.36 to 37
quotes: we show that the selective copying operation can be implemented by a circuit with constant depth
The stack on the right side can be implemented by a comparing unitary followed by a controlled copy
assertions.certainty_reason: A diagrammatic argument, not a stated theorem.

assertions.value: The paper proves, using vec(ABC) = (CT ⊗ A)vec(B), that the linear layer-wise transformation of a multi-channel GCN can be implemented by applying the block-encoding of the normalized adjacency matrix and a parameterized quantum circuit on the two registers Reg(i) and Reg(k).
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Eqs. (C1) to (C8), p.42 to 43
quotes: Using vec(ABC) = (CT ⊗ A)vec(B) (A, B,C are matrices)

the layer-specific trainable weight matrix and normalized adjacency matrix multiplied on the node feature matrix can be implemented by applying the block-encoding of the normalized adjacency matrix and a parameterized quantum circuit on the two quantum registers Reg(i) and Reg(k) respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved in Appendix C, p.42 to 43, with the identity it rests on quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The block-encoding acts probabilistically: the desired state comes with an orthogonal '+ ...' part (p.10), and normalization factors are omitted (footnote 5, p.8).

assertions.value: The authors state that predicted labels are extracted from the output state by quantum state tomography, followed by a softmax on the estimated amplitudes, and that the cost function is the negative inner product with a label state evaluated by the Modified Hadamard test.
quotes: To extract the predicted labels from the output state |ψout⟩, quantum state tomography techniques are employed.
The cost function can be evaluated via the "Modified Hadamard test" [52, 53].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its inference and training procedure, Section 3.1.3 p.11.
assertions.reader_inference: Tomography cost is not part of the complexity tables, which cover a forward pass and one cost evaluation.

assertions.value: The authors cite the Modified Hadamard test as estimating an inner product with additive precision ε using controlled applications of the two unitaries of order log(1/δ) divided by ε squared times, with probability 1−δ, and state that it needs only one additional qubit.
quotes: with additive precision ε using controlled applications of U1 and U2 O log(1/δ) ε2 times, with probability 1−δ
as the Modified Hadamard test requires only one additional qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result (refs. 52, 53).

assertions.value: The authors apply the non-linear activation with Nonlinear Transformation of Complex Amplitudes (NTCA) for a two-layer GCN, and leave the use of other techniques and the detailed analysis for future work.
quotes: the element-wise non-linear activation function can be applied using an established technique called Nonlinear Transformation of Complex Amplitudes (NTCA)[49]
we leave this and the detailed analysis for future work
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit, Section 3.1.2 p.9.

assertions.value: The authors leave for future work reusing the data-encoding ancillary qubits for the block-encoding, and the interplay between the depth of the weight-matrix PQC and the depth of the block-encoding circuit.

is an interesting topic for future research

assertions.value: The authors claim that by incorporating the inductive bias of graph-structured data, their Quantum GNN can potentially operate with fewer parameters than its problem-agnostic counterpart, potentially leading to more efficient training and less overfitting.
quotes: By incorporating the inductive bias into the architecture, our Quantum GNN can potentially operate with fewer parameters than its problem-agnostic counterpart.
This can potentially lead to more efficient training and less overfitting

quotes: These complexity results suggest that our quantum GNN frameworks have the potential to efficiently process large-scale graphs that are intractable for classical GNNs
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' conclusion going beyond the SGC and LGC analyses.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [12] and earlier work, that classical GNNs face memory limits on giant graphs, sparse matrix operations that are inefficient on GPUs optimized for dense operations, and subsampling whose subgraphs may not preserve the semantics of the whole graph or give reliable gradients.
quotes: One major challenge is the memory limitations that arise when handling giant graphs.
which pose challenges for efficient computation on modern hardware like GPUs that are optimized for dense matrix operations1 [12]
it is challenging to guarantee that these subgraphs preserve the semantics of the entire graph and provide reliable gradients for training GNNs [12]
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited classical claims.

assertions.value: The authors define the key property of GNNs as permutation equivariance, and state that the convolutional, attentional and message-passing flavours offer increasing expressivity at the cost of reduced scalability.
quotes: The key defining property of GNNs is permutation equivariance.
offer increasing levels of expressivity, albeit comes at the cost of reduced scalability

quotes: For data encoding, Hu et al. use N separate quantum circuits (N is the number of nodes), with each circuit encoding the features of a single node.
our work coherently encodes all N node features into a single quantum state on two entangled registers
while Zheng et al. focus on numerical simulations without theoretical analysis

papers.title_in_file: Can Variational Quantum Algorithms Demonstrate Quantum Advantages? Time Really Matters
papers.what_it_is: An analysis paper that argues gradient cost in VQAs scales with the parameter number (Theorem 1), derives gate-layer depths for UCCSD and HEA (Theorems 2 and 3), and estimates ideal VQA wall-clock time against classical simulation.

existing.note: The theorem statement is now quoted in full. The proof assumes a specific circuit form, each parameter entering as (cos θ I − i sin θ P) times a fixed gate, treats the term functions as unknown, and only excludes that some gradient elements are linear combinations of the others; that limits what the theorem covers.
existing.value: The paper states as Theorem 1 that for a general ansatz with L independent parameters and a cost function defined as the expectation value under some Hamiltonian, at least O(L) cost-function evaluations are needed to obtain the gradient; the proof takes the circuit as a product of gates of the form cos θl I − i sin θl Pl times an unparameterized gate, assumes the term functions are unknown, and shows that no gradient element is a linear combination of the others.
existing.anchor: Section 3, Theorem 1 and its proof, p.7 to 9
quotes: Theorem 1. For a general ansatz U (θ) with L independent parameters, and the cost function defined as the expectation value under some Hamiltonian H, we need at least O(L) times for evaluating the cost function to obtain the gradient.
U (θ) = Ul(θl)Wl = (cos θlI − i sin θlPl)Wl
We assume {fpq} are unknown.
Due to the unknown functions {fpq}, unknown elements must be a linear combination of known gradients.
existing.certainty_reason: A stated theorem whose proof only rules out linear relations among gradient elements under an assumed circuit form; it is not a general query lower bound.
existing.reader_inference: The paper itself cites [42] that backpropagation scaling is possible with multiple copies of the ansatz, so the bound holds only for the single-copy, linear-reuse setting the proof treats.

existing.note: Section 5 lists more that is ignored: hardware initialization and readout time and trainability as well as noise, connectivity and reachability, with the stated aim of showing the best time scaling.
existing.value: The authors state that the time-cost analysis is in an ideal setting that does not consider noise, qubit connectivity or reachability; in the total time cost section they also ignore the time for initializing the hardware and reading out the outcomes and limitations like trainability, to show the best time-scaling of VQAs; and they state that the work does not aim to deny the potential of VQAs.
existing.anchor: Section 1, p.2; Section 5, p.13; Abstract, p.1
quotes: we do not consider realistic limitations on VQAs like noise, qubit connectivity, reachability, etc.
the time for initializing the hardware and reading out the outcomes, as well as limitations for VQAs like reachability and trainability, are all ignored
The goal of ignoring these factors is to show the "best" time-scaling performance of VQAs.
this work does not aim to deny the potential of VQAs
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope, Section 1 p.2 and Section 5 p.13.

existing.note: The one-year figure comes from the UCCSD estimate (Fig. 5) under assumed gate times of 30 ns and 60 ns, and the paper reads the smallest sampling-times-iterations product as one optimization step, so the year is per step at the chemical-accuracy sampling level.
existing.value: The authors report, for the UCCSD ansatz with assumed single- and two-qubit gate times of 30 ns and 60 ns, that even at about 20 qubits VQAs easily reached the 1-year time, and that the time for one step of parameter optimization at the chemical-accuracy sampling level comes at the level of 1 year on an ideal quantum computer.
existing.anchor: Section 4, p.10; Fig. 5 caption, p.13 to 14
quotes: The time of applying a single- and two-qubit gate are tsingle = 30 ns and tdouble = 60 ns
Even at a scaling of about 20 qubits, VQAs easily reached the 1-year time.
can be viewed as the time for performing one step of parameter optimization, which comes at the level of 1 year
existing.certainty_reason: A modelled time estimate from assumed gate times and sample counts, not a measurement or theorem.

assertions.value: The paper proves as Theorem 2 that, for a many-body system with no spin-orbitals and ne electrons under the first-order Trotter expansion, the UCCSD single-qubit gate layer depth is 6 times the number of single-excitation terms plus 24 times the number of double-excitation terms, with a two-qubit layer depth also given in closed form.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, Theorem 2 and proof, p.11 to 12
quotes: Theorem 2. For a many-body system with no spin-orbitals and ne electrons, the gate layer depth for the UCCSD ansatz under the first-order Trotter expansion is: lsingle =6Cn1e Cn1o−ne + 24Cn2e Cn2o−ne
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 with its conditions (Jordan-Wigner mapping, first-order Trotter) stated and proved on p.11 to 12.
assertions.reader_inference: The count assumes the circuit of Fig. 3(a) for each Pauli exponential, with no gate parallelism across terms.

assertions.value: The paper states as Theorem 3 that the HEA with P blocks has single-qubit layer depth 3P and two-qubit layer depth nP, and it has 3nP parameters.
quotes: Theorem 3. For the HEA described above with P blocks, we have: lsingle = 3P, ldouble = nP.
LHEA = 3nP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows directly from the HEA definition in Eqs. (16) to (18), p.6 to 7, and is stated as Theorem 3, p.12.

assertions.value: The authors state that backpropagation cannot be implemented directly for QNNs because a QNN does not record the inter-layer state, and cite a reference that backpropagation scaling for training QNNs is only possible with multiple copies of the ansatz.
quotes: the backpropagation algorithm cannot be implemented directly because a QNN is a parameterized unitary transformation that maps an initial state to the ansatz, without recording to inter-layer state
the backpropagation scaling for training QNNs is only possible when we have multiple copies of the ansatz
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument plus a cited result (ref. 42).

assertions.value: The authors argue that because gradient cost depends on the number of parameters, increasing parameters to improve performance, a strategy that works for classical NNs, is not a good choice in VQAs, and that applying VQAs would be challenging as the parameter number grows with problem size.
quotes: This dependency heavily limits the scalability of VQAs.
However, scalability limitation makes increasing parameters not a good choice in VQAs.
Since the parameter number naturally grows with the problem size or complexity, applying VQAs would be challenging.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' argument drawn from Theorem 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that reaching sampling error ε needs of order 1/ε squared samples, so about ten to the sixth samples are required to reach chemical accuracy of 1.6 times ten to the minus third Hartree, and that barren plateaus can cause exponentially increased sampling times.
quotes: achieving sampling error ε will require sampling O(1/ε2) times
Then about 106 sampling times is required to reach the widely-applied chemical accuracy 1.6 × 10−3 Hartree
problems like barren plateaus can cause exponentially increased sampling times
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard estimate stated without derivation in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors show that with the parameter-shift rule and sampling error ε, the worst-case sampled gradient is the true gradient minus ε, so updating in the correct direction needs sampling accuracy tied to the scale of the gradient, and barren plateaus would then require exponential sampling times.
quotes: Then sampling accuracy is dependent on the scaling of the gradient.
While the magnitude of the gradient could be affected by the barren plateaus, exponential sampling times would be required, which is not workable in practice.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short worst-case derivation, not a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors model the total VQA time as sample time times samples per cost function times cost functions per gradient times iterations, take the sample time as the circuit running time only, ignoring initialization and readout of the order of 1 μs as comparable to about a hundred gates, and obtain a total time that grows polynomially in qubit number for a fixed product of samples and iterations.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, Eqs. (40) to (45) and (58) to (60), p.9 to 13
quotes: On current superconducting hardware, tinitial and tread together will reach the order of 1 μs [43, 44].
then we will ignore this cost and only take the circuit running time as tsample
We can see that for a fixed Nsi, the total time establishes a polynomial growth.

assertions.value: The authors estimate time for solving ground states of molecular systems with the number of electrons set to half the spin-orbitals, with the product of samples and iterations ranging from ten to the sixth to ten to the twelfth, and HEA block depths P = n and P = n squared, using 1-year and 1000-year times as benchmarks.
quotes: we consider applying VQAs to solve the ground states of different-sized molecular systems
The number of electrons is set to be ne = no/2.
Therefore, Nsi ranges from 106 to 1012.
Therefore, we will consider the following two cases: P = n and P = n2.
The 1-year and 1000-year time are given as benchmarks.

assertions.value: For classical simulation, the authors set the gate time for 10 qubits as ten to the minus third seconds, doubling with each further qubit, with no sampling required, against ten to the sixth samples for the quantum case.
quotes: We set the gate time of 10 qubits as t10 = 10−3 s and the time for n qubits is tn = t102n−10.
Sampling is not required with classical simulation. We set Nsample = 106 for quantum simulations to reach the chemical accuracy.

assertions.reader_inference: The classical model is a single-core state-vector simulator with no tensor-network or other methods; the paper notes multi-core speedups separately.

assertions.value: The authors report that the VQA and classical simulation time curves cross at a time that is at the scaling of years and increases with the number of parameters, so VQAs can only outperform classical computers when the required time exceeds it; their conclusion puts the crossing over ten to the second years with the UCCSD ansatz.

and it also increased with the number of parameters.
